paragraphs.source_en: Speaking of willfulness, it reminds me of a story about how my master came to grief through that very willfulness. To begin with, my master has no accomplishments superior to other people's, yet he insists on trying his hand at everything. At times he composes haiku and submits them to Hototogisu, at times he sends new-style poems to Myojo, at times he writes English full of mistakes; he has studied utai chanting, and for a while he even scraped away on a violin. Unfortunately, not a single one of these pursuits has amounted to anything. Still, though he is chronically weak in the stomach, once he sets about such things he becomes absurdly earnest. He sings utai in the privy, and though the neighbors have nicknamed him Professor Privy for it, he remains utterly unconcerned and keeps repeating, 'I am Taira no Munemori.' At this everyone bursts out laughing whenever they hear him, saying, 'Listen, there goes Munemori again!' For reasons known only to himself, about a month after I had moved into his house, on the day he received his monthly salary, this master came hurrying home carrying a large parcel. I wondered what he had bought. It turned out to be watercolor paints, brushes, and paper called Whatman; apparently he had resolved that from that day forward he would give up utai and haiku and devote himself solely to painting. Sure enough, from the next day on, for some time he spent every day in his study doing nothing but paint, even forgoing his afternoon nap. But when one looked at what he had finished, no one could tell what on earth he had painted. Perhaps he himself felt that the results were none too good. One day, when a friend of his who seemed to be studying aesthetics came to visit, I heard them have the following conversation:

paragraphs.source_en: It really is hard to paint well. When you look at other people's work it seems easy enough, but once you take up the brush yourself, you truly feel how difficult painting is. This was my master's lament. Indeed, that much showed an honest side of him. His friend, looking at my master's face through gold-rimmed spectacles, said, 'Naturally you cannot paint well right from the start. For one thing, shut up indoors as you are, painting only from imagination, there is no way you can produce a picture. The great Italian master Andrea del Sarto once said: "If a man would paint, he must copy nature itself. There are stars in the heavens and dew-bright blossoms on the earth; birds fly above and beasts run below; goldfish swim in ponds and crows perch on withered trees; all of nature is one magnificent living picture." If you want to paint something worthy of the name, why not try sketching from life?'
